quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the loom plan, the changeover sheet and the yarn working sheet.

questions.q: In the loom plan, what does the 'A %' column represent?
options: The percentage of production that is A-grade (first quality)
questions.explain: A % is the first-quality yield; only A-grade cloth counts towards the order, so daily output is multiplied by it after efficiency.

questions.q: In the plan, 'Packed' is computed as:
questions.explain: Packing is allowed 2 days after the finish date; arrival in Karachi is a further 4 days, and the dispatch deadline is the vessel date minus 4 days.

questions.q: The dispatch deadline for an order is:
questions.explain: Goods must leave 4 days before the vessel sails; the plan compares the finish date with this deadline to flag lateness.

questions.q: A negative value in the 'Late' column means the order will miss its vessel.
questions.explain: Late = finish − dispatch + 2; negative numbers mean the order is safe with days to spare. Positive values are the planner's alarm.

questions.q: What does the Planning II (changeover) sheet list?
options: For every calendar day, how many looms run each quality
The sizing recipe for each warp
questions.explain: The changeover sheet is a day-by-day allocation of looms to qualities, with a total that must never exceed the looms in the shed.

questions.q: A loom changeover in this lecture refers to:
options: Re-beaming a loom for the next quality when a lot finishes, which takes a day or more
Switching the loom to the night shift
questions.explain: When a lot finishes its looms are re-beamed for the next quality; the sheet allows a day or more of lost production for this.

questions.q: The yarn working sheet (Planning III) converts each quality into:
options: Warp and weft pounds per yard, then bags per loom per day
questions.explain: The sheet gives warp lb/yd and weft lb/yd and, with the production per loom per day, the bags of warp and weft each loom consumes daily.

questions.q: In the quality code 60×60/161×114, the figures 161 and 114 are the ends per inch and picks per inch.
questions.explain: The convention is warp count × weft count / ends per inch × picks per inch: Ne 60 warp and weft, 161 EPI and 114 PPI.

questions.q: Why does the Planning III text say the yarn store must hold the bags 'before the beams are sized'?
options: Because sizing is the last process
Because warping and sizing consume the warp yarn before the looms ever start
Because bags are counted after weaving
questions.explain: Warp yarn is drawn into beams at warping and sizing ahead of weaving, so the yarn must be in stock before the plan's first loom day.

questions.q: In the original workbook the 'Days' cell is rounded to:
questions.explain: The lecture notes that the Days cell rounds to the nearest half day, and that rows are chained so the next lot starts the day after the previous one finishes.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The daily-yards, date and yarn formulas of the plan, and how each result moves when an input changes.

questions.q: Daily yards of a quality are computed as Σ(rpm × widths × looms × 24 × 60) ÷ 36 ÷ PPI × efficiency × A %. The '÷ 36' converts:
questions.explain: Picks per day ÷ PPI gives inches of cloth; dividing by 36 turns inches into yards.

questions.q: If the picks per inch of a quality are increased, with the same loom speed and efficiency, the daily yards will:
questions.explain: More picks are needed for every inch of cloth, so the same picks per day produce fewer yards. PPI is in the denominator of the formula.

questions.q: Days required for an order are found as:
questions.explain: Days = quantity ÷ daily output. Multiplying would give a meaningless figure; dividing by looms alone ignores the speed and construction.

questions.q: The warp lb/yd formula is ends × width × (1 + crimp) ÷ (840 × Ne). The (1 + crimp) term allows for:
options: The extra yarn length taken up by bending over and under the weft
questions.explain: A yarn in the fabric is longer than the fabric it lies in because of crimp, so more yarn is consumed than the fabric length suggests.

questions.q: Production per loom per day in yards = rpm × eff × 1440 ÷ (PPI × 36) × widths, where 1440 is the minutes in a day.
questions.explain: 24 × 60 = 1,440 minutes; rpm × eff × 1440 is picks per day, which divided by PPI × 36 gives yards, times the number of widths on the loom.

questions.q: Warp bags per loom per day are obtained from:
questions.explain: Pounds of warp per day = production × warp lb/yd; a bag is 100 lb, so dividing by 100 gives bags. Thus 263.9 × 0.2368 ÷ 100 = 0.625 bags.

questions.q: Late is computed as finish − dispatch + 2. The '+ 2' is there because:
options: Two days are needed for packing after the finish date
The vessel always sails two days late
Two days are lost in changeover
It is a safety margin for weaving
questions.explain: The goods cannot be dispatched until packing (2 days) is done, so the finish date is effectively 2 days later when compared with the dispatch deadline.

questions.q: Adding looms to a quality on the plan will:
options: Raise daily yards and shorten the days, pulling the finish date earlier
Raise daily yards but leave the finish date unchanged
questions.explain: Looms multiply daily output; more output means fewer days and an earlier finish — one of the three remedies the lecture gives for a positive Late value.

questions.q: If the weft crimp is raised from 9 % to 12 % in the yarn sheet, the weft lb/yd will:
questions.explain: Weft lb/yd scales with (1 + crimp): 1.12 ÷ 1.09 = 1.0275, so about 2.75 % more weft is consumed per yard.

questions.q: The daily warp and weft requirement in Planning III is found by multiplying the per-loom bags by the looms running each day from the changeover sheet.
questions.explain: Bags per loom per day × looms running that day gives the day's requirement; summing by month and comparing with yarn booked is the sheet's purpose.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Run the plan's arithmetic: daily yards, days, dates, lateness and yarn in bags.

questions.q: Four looms weave 60×60/161×114 68" at 800 rpm, 94 % efficiency, 1 width each, with 96 % A-grade. Daily yards = rpm × widths × looms × 1440 ÷ 36 ÷ PPI × eff × A %. Answer to the nearest yard.
The 114" quality produces 1,265 yd per day and the order is 32,000 yd. How many days are required? Answer to one decimal.
An order starts on day 9 and needs 25.9 days. On what day number will it arrive in Karachi (finish + 2 days packing + 4 days transit)?
questions.explain: Finish = 9 + 25.9 = 34.9; packed 36.9; in Karachi 40.9.

questions.q: A lot finishes on day 43.2 and its vessel sails on day 52. Compute Late = finish − (vessel − 4) + 2. Answer to one decimal (negative means safe).
questions.explain: Dispatch deadline = 52 − 4 = 48; Late = 43.2 − 48 + 2 = −2.8 days, so the order is safe by nearly three days.

questions.q: Warp lb/yd for 60×60/161×114 at 98" width with 9 % warp crimp: ends × width × (1 + crimp) ÷ (840 × Ne). Answer to four decimals.
Weft lb/yd for the 114" width of 60×60/161×114 with 9 % weft crimp: PPI × width × (1 + crimp) ÷ (840 × Ne). Answer to four decimals.
questions.explain: 114 picks × 114 in = 12,996 yd of weft per yard of cloth; × 1.09 = 14,166; ÷ 50,400 = 0.2811 lb per yard.

questions.q: A loom runs at 800 rpm, 94 % efficiency, on a 114 PPI quality, single width. Production per day = rpm × eff × 1440 ÷ (PPI × 36) × widths. Answer to one decimal.
A 68" loom makes 263.9 yd/day and the warp weighs 0.2368 lb/yd. How many 100 lb bags of warp does it use per day? Answer to three decimals.
Eight 114" looms use 0.464 weft bags per loom per day each and run for 26 days. The weft to hold in stock is about:
questions.explain: 0.464 × 8 × 26 = 96.5 bags, which must be rounded up to 97 whole bags; 96 would leave the last day short.

questions.q: On day 10 of the changeover table the 68" lot 1 runs 6 looms, the 98" 6 looms and the 114" 8 looms. The total running is:
questions.explain: 6 + 6 + 8 = 20 looms, the peak of the plan. The totals of 12 and 14 belong to other days in the table.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Planning decisions in the weaving office: late orders, idle looms, chained lots and the yarn store.

questions.q: The plan shows Late = +3.5 for a quality. Which is NOT one of the lecture's remedies?
questions.explain: The lecture names adding looms, raising speed or negotiating the vessel. Lowering A % would reduce usable output and make the order later still.

questions.q: The changeover table shows only 4–6 looms running on days 40–60 in a 20-loom shed. The planner should:
options: Shut the mill for those days
Treat the idle looms as capacity for new bookings
questions.explain: Idle looms are the opportunity for new bookings — the lecture says Planning IV takes this up with a month-long simulation.

questions.q: A second lot of the 68" quality is chained to start the day after the first lot finishes (day 44.2). The reason for chaining rather than starting both together is that:
options: The same looms are reused after the first lot, so they cannot run both lots at once
The customer wants the lots on different vessels
The yarn store has limited bags
questions.explain: The second lot uses the looms freed by the first, so it cannot begin until those looms finish and are re-beamed.

questions.q: The daily total of looms on the changeover sheet may exceed the looms in the shed for a day or two if the orders are urgent.
questions.explain: The lecture is explicit: the daily total must never exceed the looms in the shed. An urgent order needs speed, a later vessel or looms taken from another quality.

questions.q: Six 98" looms are planned for 12 days at 0.675 warp bags and 0.478 weft bags per loom per day. The store holds 45 warp bags and 40 weft bags. What should the planner do?
options: Order about 4 more warp bags; weft is sufficient
Order more weft; warp is sufficient
questions.explain: Warp needed 0.675 × 6 × 12 = 48.6 → 49 bags (short by 4); weft 0.478 × 72 = 34.4 → 35 bags, covered by the 40 in stock.

questions.q: A merchandiser asks why an order with Late = −24 is not being finished even earlier. The best reply is:
options: It is already safe by 24 days; moving looms to the orders with positive Late values is the better use of capacity
Negative Late means it is impossible to finish
The vessel must be moved later
questions.explain: A large negative Late means ample margin. Capacity is better spent on orders at risk; over-serving a safe order gains nothing.

questions.q: The plan assumes each lot's looms are re-beamed in one day. If changeovers actually take two days, the effect on the chained second lot is:
options: Its start and finish both move a day later, reducing its margin
No effect, because Late is computed from the vessel
questions.explain: The chained lot starts after the changeover; a longer changeover delays the start, the finish and therefore eats into the Late margin.

questions.q: If the yarn booked for a month is less than the monthly requirement summed from the daily plan, the shortfall will surface as looms standing idle for want of beams.
questions.explain: The yarn sheet exists to compare requirement against booked yarn month by month; any gap means beams cannot be sized in time and looms stop.

questions.q: Two qualities compete for 6 free looms: a 98" sheeting with Late = +5 and a 114" sheeting with Late = −19. The looms should go to:
options: The 98" quality, to remove its lateness
The 114" quality, because wider cloth earns more
questions.explain: The positive Late value is the alarm; extra looms raise its daily yards and pull its finish before the dispatch deadline, while the 114" order already has 19 days to spare.

questions.q: A planner reads the quantity column in metres but divides by daily output in yards. The days will be:
questions.explain: A metre is 1.0936 yd, so the order in yards is 9.4 % larger than the figure in metres; dividing the metre figure by yards per day gives too few days.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step planning problems across all three sheets, with the slips that catch students in exams.

questions.q: A quality needs 65,000 yd. Six looms run at 800 rpm, 94 % efficiency, 114 PPI, single width, 96 % A-grade. How many days are needed? Answer to one decimal.
The same order (6 looms, 1,520 yd/day, 65,000 yd) starts on day 1 and its vessel sails on day 48. Compute Late = finish − (vessel − 4) + 2, where finish = 1 + days. Answer to one decimal.
questions.explain: Days = 42.8; finish = 43.8; dispatch = 44; Late = 43.8 − 44 + 2 = +1.8 — the order is late and needs more looms or a later vessel.

questions.q: For the order above (65,000 yd, 1,520 yd/day with 6 looms, start day 1, vessel day 48), how many looms would bring Late to exactly 0? Treat daily yards as proportional to looms and answer to one decimal.
questions.explain: Late = 0 needs finish = 44 − 2 = 42, so days = 41 and daily yards = 65,000 ÷ 41 = 1,585; at 253.3 yd per loom that is 6.3 looms — so 7 looms in practice.

questions.q: A student computes daily yards as rpm × looms × 1440 × PPI ÷ 36 and gets a number in the hundreds of thousands. The error is:
options: PPI should divide, not multiply — more picks per inch means fewer inches of cloth
questions.explain: Picks per day ÷ PPI gives inches of cloth. Multiplying by PPI inflates the figure by PPI² and is a classic slip.

questions.q: A 98" loom makes 197.9 yd/day; warp 0.3412 lb/yd, weft 0.2416 lb/yd. What are the total bags (warp + weft) per loom per day? Answer to three decimals.
The 98" loom produces fewer yards per day (197.9) than the 68" loom (263.9) for the same construction. The reason in the yarn sheet is:
options: Wider looms run at a lower adjusted speed
The 98" quality has more picks per inch
questions.explain: Both have 114 PPI; the sheet uses the adjusted loom speed, and wider looms run slower, so picks per day and therefore yards fall.

questions.q: From the changeover table, looms running on days 1, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 are 12, 12, 20, 14, 14, 6, 4 and 4. If the shed has 20 looms, what is the average number of idle looms across these eight sample days? Answer to two decimals.
questions.explain: Total idle = 160 − 86 = 74 loom-days over 8 days = 9.25 idle looms on average — the capacity Planning IV sets out to fill.

questions.q: A planner raises efficiency in the plan from 94 % to 98 % to make a late order look safe. The weakness of this is:
options: Efficiency cannot be changed on paper — if the looms do not actually achieve 98 % the order will still be late
Efficiency does not affect daily yards
questions.explain: The plan is only as good as its inputs; an efficiency the shed cannot deliver hides the problem rather than solving it. The real remedies are looms, speed or vessel.

questions.q: The 122" quality has a warp of 0.4131 lb/yd and makes 164.9 yd per day per loom. If 10 looms run for a 30-day month, how many warp bags are consumed? Answer to one decimal.
questions.explain: Per loom per day 164.9 × 0.4131 ÷ 100 = 0.681 bags; × 10 looms × 30 days = 204.4 bags for the month.

questions.q: If a lot's finish date is later than its arrival in Karachi date, the plan contains an error.
questions.explain: In Karachi = finish + 6 days (2 packing + 4 transit), so it can never precede the finish. A reversal means a date or formula has been overwritten.
